title: Your toolkit: editor, terminal, Git and DevTools
intro: A good developer toolkit removes friction from everyday work. In this lesson, you’ll set up IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition as the default IDE for the whole course, learn the terminal and Git basics, and get comfortable with the browser’s DevTools.
body:
## One IDE for the whole course

For this course, **IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is the default IDE**. We’ll use it for both frontend and backend work: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Java and Spring Boot.

~~~callout ide Shortcuts worth learning on day one
- **Shift Shift** — Search Everywhere (files, classes, actions)
- **Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + A** — find any action by name
- **Alt + Enter** — quick fixes and imports
- **Shift + F10** — run · **Shift + F9** — debug
- **Alt + F12** — open the built-in terminal
~~~

Using one IDE throughout the course keeps the workflow consistent. You don’t need to learn a different editor just because you switch from frontend code to backend code. The same project navigation, search, terminal, Git integration and keyboard shortcuts stay available across the stack.

### Installing IntelliJ IDEA

The simplest option is **JetBrains Toolbox**, which lets you install and manage JetBrains products from one place. You can also download IntelliJ IDEA directly from JetBrains and install it normally.

After installation, open IntelliJ IDEA and create or open a project. The IDE will recognise the technologies in your project and provide the appropriate editing and navigation features.

### A few settings and habits worth learning

You don’t need to customise everything on day one. Start with a few habits that make everyday development faster.

- **Reformat on save:** configure the IDE to reformat your code when you save. Consistent formatting makes code easier to read and keeps unnecessary formatting changes out of reviews.
- **Terminal tool window:** IntelliJ IDEA has a built-in terminal, so you can run commands such as `npm`, `git`, `java` or other project tools without leaving the IDE.
- **Built-in Git tool window:** use the Git interface to review changed files, inspect diffs, create commits, switch branches and perform common Git operations.
- **Search Everywhere:** press **Shift twice** to search for files, classes, actions, settings and other things across the IDE. This is one of the most useful shortcuts to learn early.
- **Keymap:** learn the shortcuts for your operating system and customise them only when necessary. You don’t need to memorise everything; start with navigation, search, save, reformat and Git-related actions.

The goal is not to avoid the terminal or Git commands. The goal is to understand what is happening while using whichever interface is fastest for the task.

### What about VS Code?

**VS Code is a perfectly good alternative** if you already use it and are comfortable with it. You don’t need to switch editors just because this course uses IntelliJ IDEA as its default.

The important thing is to understand the development workflow and tools rather than becoming dependent on a particular editor.

---

## The terminal

The terminal is a text-based interface for running commands on your computer. Developers use it constantly because many development tools are command-line based.

You’ll commonly use commands such as:

~~~text
pwd
ls
cd project
mkdir new-folder
npm install
npm run dev
git status
~~~

On Windows, some commands have different equivalents. For example, `dir` is commonly used instead of `ls`.

You don’t need to memorise hundreds of commands. Learn the small set you use regularly and understand what each command does.

A typical workflow might look like this:

~~~text
cd my-project
npm install
npm run dev
~~~

The terminal is especially useful when working with package managers, build tools, development servers, Git, Docker and backend tooling.

---

## Git: your safety net

Git is a version control system. It records changes to your code so you can inspect what happened, create separate lines of development and collaborate with other developers.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Where your changes live", "nodes": [{"id": "wd", "label": "Working directory", "sub": "files you edit", "kind": "file"}, {"id": "st", "label": "Staging area", "sub": "next commit"}, {"id": "repo", "label": "Local repository", "sub": "commit history", "kind": "db", "highlight": true}, {"id": "gh", "label": "GitHub", "sub": "remote: origin", "kind": "cloud"}], "edges": [{"from": "wd", "to": "st", "label": "git add"}, {"from": "st", "to": "repo", "label": "git commit"}, {"from": "repo", "to": "gh", "label": "git push"}, {"from": "gh", "to": "wd", "label": "git pull", "dashed": true}]}
~~~

The basic concepts are:

- **Repository (repo):** the project tracked by Git.
- **Working tree:** the files you are currently editing.
- **Staging:** selecting changes that should become part of the next commit.
- **Commit:** a snapshot of selected changes with a message explaining what changed.
- **Branch:** an independent line of development.
- **Merge:** combining changes from different branches.
- **Remote:** a repository hosted somewhere else, such as GitHub.
- **Push:** send local commits to a remote repository.
- **Pull:** retrieve changes from a remote repository.

A simple workflow looks like this:

~~~text
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add login form"
git push
~~~

Good commit messages describe the change clearly. For example:

~~~text
Add email validation to registration form
Fix incorrect task status mapping
Update project creation endpoint
~~~

Avoid messages such as `fix`, `changes`, or `stuff`. Your future self and your teammates will thank you.

Git is not just a backup system. It gives you a history of the project and makes experimentation much safer.

---

## GitHub and remote repositories

Git can work entirely locally, but most professional projects also use a remote Git repository. GitHub is one common choice.

A typical project may have a local repository on your computer and a remote repository on GitHub. You can commit locally while working and push your commits when you want to share them.

This also enables collaboration through branches, pull requests and code reviews.

---

## Browser DevTools

When you build frontend applications, the browser itself becomes one of your most important debugging tools.

Open DevTools by right-clicking a page and choosing **Inspect**, or by using the browser’s keyboard shortcut.

The most useful panels to learn first are:

### Elements

Inspect the current HTML structure and see which CSS rules are applied to an element. You can temporarily change HTML and CSS to experiment with a page.

Remember that changes made directly in DevTools are temporary. They help you investigate a problem, but they do not automatically modify your source files.

### Console

The Console shows JavaScript errors, warnings and messages. You can also run JavaScript expressions directly in it.

If a button does nothing, a useful first step is often to check whether the Console contains an error.

### Network

The Network panel shows requests made by the browser. You can inspect URLs, methods, status codes, request headers, response headers, payloads and timing.

This is particularly important when working with APIs. If your frontend says that something went wrong, the Network panel can tell you whether the request was actually sent and what the server returned.

### Application / Storage

The Application panel helps you inspect browser storage and application-related data such as cookies, local storage and session storage.

These tools become especially useful when debugging authentication and client-side state.

### Device toolbar

The device toolbar lets you simulate different viewport sizes and test responsive layouts. It is useful, but it is not a replacement for testing on a real phone.

---

## A practical daily workflow

A productive development workflow is usually a sequence of small, repeatable steps:

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "A daily loop", "steps": [{"label": "Pull", "sub": "git pull — start from the latest code"}, {"label": "Branch", "sub": "git switch -c feature/…"}, {"label": "Code & run", "sub": "IntelliJ + DevTools"}, {"label": "Commit", "sub": "small, meaningful steps"}, {"label": "Push & PR", "sub": "review before merge"}]}
~~~

1. Open the project in IntelliJ IDEA.
2. Check the current Git status.
3. Read the relevant code before changing it.
4. Make a small change.
5. Run the application or relevant tests.
6. Use the browser DevTools when debugging frontend behaviour.
7. Inspect the Git diff.
8. Commit a focused change with a useful message.
9. Push the branch when it is ready to share.

The tools are most useful when they work together. IntelliJ IDEA helps you navigate and edit the code, the terminal runs development commands, Git tracks changes, and DevTools helps you understand what the browser is doing.

---

## Setup checklist

Before continuing with the course, make sure you have:

- **IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition** installed.
- **Git** installed and configured.
- **Node.js LTS** installed for frontend development.
- **Java 21 JDK** installed for the Java and Spring Boot parts of the course.
- A GitHub account if you want to publish repositories and collaborate remotely.
- A browser with DevTools available.

You do not need to master all of these tools immediately. The goal is to become comfortable enough that the tools stop being obstacles and let you focus on solving problems.

---

## The mental model

Think of your development toolkit as a set of complementary tools rather than a collection of unrelated software:

~~~text
IntelliJ IDEA → edit, navigate, search and manage the project
Terminal      → run commands and development tools
Git           → track and share changes
DevTools      → inspect and debug the browser
~~~

As the course gets more advanced, you’ll use these tools together constantly. Learning them now will make the later frontend, backend and full-stack lessons much easier.
takeaways: IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is the default IDE for the whole course, including frontend and backend development.
JetBrains Toolbox or a direct download are both straightforward ways to install IntelliJ IDEA.
Learn a few high-value IntelliJ IDEA habits: reformat on save, the Terminal tool window, the built-in Git tool window, Search Everywhere with double Shift, and useful keymap shortcuts.
VS Code is a perfectly good optional alternative if you already use it.
The terminal is an essential part of modern development, especially for package managers, build tools, development servers and Git.
Git tracks your project history through repositories, staging, commits, branches and remotes.
Browser DevTools help you inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, investigate network requests and test responsive layouts.
A good workflow combines the IDE, terminal, Git and DevTools rather than treating them as separate tools.

quiz.question: Which IDE is the default for this course?
quiz.explanation: IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is the default IDE for the whole course, covering both frontend and backend development.

quiz.question: What is the quickest way to open Search Everywhere in IntelliJ IDEA?
quiz.explanation: Pressing Shift twice opens Search Everywhere, which can search for files, classes, actions, settings and more.

quiz.question: What does a Git commit represent?
options: A snapshot of selected changes with a message
quiz.explanation: A commit records a snapshot of staged changes together with a message describing the change.

quiz.question: Which DevTools panel is most useful for investigating an API request and its response?
quiz.explanation: The Network panel shows requests, methods, status codes, headers, payloads, responses and timing.

quiz.question: Which statement about VS Code is correct?
options: It must not be used during the course.
It is required for frontend development.
It is a fine optional alternative if you already use it.
It can only be used for JavaScript.
quiz.explanation: IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is the course default, but VS Code remains a perfectly good optional alternative.

exercise.title: Check commit messages and summarize changes
exercise.task: Create two top-level functions named `isGoodCommitMessage(message)` and `summarize(files)`. `isGoodCommitMessage` must validate the first line according to all of these rules: it is not empty, is at most 50 characters, does not end with a period, and starts with a capital letter; when there are additional lines, the second line must be empty. `summarize(files)` receives an array of objects containing `path` and `status` and must return an object containing one property for every status that appears, with the number of files having that status. The tests expect the functions to be available directly and do not require console output.
exercise.hint: Split the message with `split('\n')` and validate `lines[0]`. A regular expression such as `/^[A-Z]/` checks that the subject starts with an uppercase English letter. For `summarize`, use an object as a counter and increment the property matching each file's status.

tests.name: It accepts a good commit message
tests.code: return isGoodCommitMessage('Add task creation form') === true && isGoodCommitMessage('Fix API error handling\n\nExplain why the error handling changed') === true;

tests.name: It rejects bad subject lines
tests.code: return isGoodCommitMessage('') === false && isGoodCommitMessage('add task creation form') === false && isGoodCommitMessage('Fix task creation form.') === false;

tests.name: It enforces the subject length
tests.code: const good = 'A'.repeat(50); const bad = 'A'.repeat(51); return isGoodCommitMessage(good) === true && isGoodCommitMessage(bad) === false;

tests.name: It requires a blank second line
It counts file statuses
tests.code: const result = summarize([{ path: 'a.js', status: 'modified' }, { path: 'b.js', status: 'added' }, { path: 'c.js', status: 'modified' }, { path: 'd.css', status: 'deleted' }]); return result.modified === 2 && result.added === 1 && result.deleted === 1 && Object.keys(result).length === 3;
